title: Your student's honor (Avot 4:12)
hookLine: a correction in front of the whole room: let your student's honor be as dear to you as your own
tomorrow: three crowns, and one above them all. which one can anyone wear?

cards: The note was right. The timing was wrong. A team lead corrects the new intern's slide in front of the whole meeting, and the intern's face goes red, and the room goes quiet in that particular way.
Now what? The correction stands. But something else got knocked over, and it belongs to the person who knows the least in the room.
One question for today: whose honor do you guard?

teach.h: A LADDER, READ FROM THE BOTTOM.
teach.b: Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua answers with a ladder. Let your student's honor be as dear to you as your own. Your colleague's honor, as dear as reverence for your teacher.
And reverence for your teacher, as reverence for heaven. Read it from the bottom.

teach.h: THE STUDENT GETS YOUR OWN HONOR.
teach.b: The student, the one below you, gets your own honor, not a lesser one. That's the surprise. A ladder could have started at the top.
This one starts by guarding the person at the bottom. So the answer to the red-faced intern isn't take back the note. It's give it where their honor is safe.
Here's a neighbor who'd recognize this.

In the Christian New Testament, Paul writes to the believers in Rome, and in the King James words: "in honour preferring one another." Both texts turn honor around, so it flows down and sideways, not only up.
Both ask you to treat someone else's dignity as if it were yours, or more than yours.
And an honest difference: Avot builds a ladder inside a house of learning, student, colleague, teacher, rising to reverence for heaven. Paul's line has no ladder.
It's written to a community of believers in Christ, asking each one to put the other first, as family. Same direction of honor, two different houses.

how: In traditional Jewish study a teacher is careful not to shame a student in public, and many teachers speak of what they learned from their students as well as from their own teachers.

o: the grades and prizes a student earns in school
the dignity of someone you teach, guarded like your own
the respect a student owes to every teacher

games.q: the ladder of honor — tap the pairs.
p: put one another first in honor

s: Avot's ladder of honor only protects the people at the top
it starts at the bottom: your student's honor is as dear as your own.
Avot and Paul's letter say exactly the same thing
both turn honor toward others; Avot builds a ladder of learning, Paul writes to a community as family.
honoring a student can still include correcting them
the note can stand; the saying guards where and how it's given.

games.q: you coach a kids' soccer team. your newest player keeps drifting offside, and the parents on the sideline are watching. what fits Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua's ladder?
o: fix it quietly at the next break, the way you'd want to be corrected.
say nothing at all, since honoring a student means no corrections.
call it out loud so the whole team learns the rule at once.
games.why: the ladder doesn't cancel teaching. it says the student's honor is as dear as yours, so the correction goes where that honor stays safe.

practice: Count, on your fingers, three people younger or newer than you who've taught you something: a kid sibling, a new coworker, a student, a teammate. Give each one a full breath, and with it, the specific thing they taught you.

wordCard.voice: Your student's honor. Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua: let it be as dear to you as your own, and climb the ladder from there.

orig.note: Hebrew: your student's honor. kavod is honor, weight, dignity.

carryVoice: For the road: honor the student, the newest person in any room. Day thirty-five of sixty, done.

sources.ref: Mishnah Avot 4:12 (Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua: let your student's honor be as dear to you as your own)
